question.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=10$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 8 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{3}{5}{x}_{1}+\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{3}{4}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -\frac{3}{4} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall that if A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of a 3×2 matrix A, then

  • Σ is a 3×2 matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • U is an orthogonal 3×3 matrix,

  • V is an orthogonal 2×2 matrix.

From the matrix Σ, we deduce that σ1=10 and σ2=0. Also, the columns v1 and v2 of V give us the right singular vectors of A.

Therefore, we can compute the first column of U as follows:

u1=1σ1Av1=110[608000][10]=110[680]=[35450]

Since the second singular value is σ2=0, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of U. But we know that U must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors

u=[x1x2x3]

such that u1⋅u=0 and ‖u‖=1.

Solving u1⋅u=0, which is equivalent to 35x1+45x2=0⟹3x1+4x2=0, we get the general solution

[x1−34x1x3]=x1[1−340]⏟b1+x3[001]⏟b2,

where x1 and x3 are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions b1 and b2 are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of U:

u2=[45−350]u3=[001]

So, the matrix U could be the following: U=[3545045−350001]

last_observation.name: Question 11
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the First Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix: Advanced Cases
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=10$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 8 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{3}{5}{x}_{1}+\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{3}{4}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -\frac{3}{4} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that if A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of a 3×2 matrix A, then

  • Σ is a 3×2 matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • U is an orthogonal 3×3 matrix,

  • V is an orthogonal 2×2 matrix.

From the matrix Σ, we deduce that σ1=10 and σ2=0. Also, the columns v1 and v2 of V give us the right singular vectors of A.

Therefore, we can compute the first column of U as follows:

u1=1σ1Av1=110[608000][10]=110[680]=[35450]

Since the second singular value is σ2=0, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of U. But we know that U must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors

u=[x1x2x3]

such that u1⋅u=0 and ‖u‖=1.

Solving u1⋅u=0, which is equivalent to 35x1+45x2=0⟹3x1+4x2=0, we get the general solution

[x1−34x1x3]=x1[1−340]⏟b1+x3[001]⏟b2,

where x1 and x3 are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions b1 and b2 are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of U:

u2=[45−350]u3=[001]

feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=10$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 8 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{3}{5}{x}_{1}+\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{3}{4}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -\frac{3}{4} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

question.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{4}{5}{x}_{1}+\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{4} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ \frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that if A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of a 3×2 matrix A, then

  • Σ is a 3×2 matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • U is an orthogonal 3×3 matrix,

  • V is an orthogonal 2×2 matrix.

From the matrix Σ, we deduce that σ1=5 and σ2=0. Also, the columns v1 and v2 of V give us the right singular vectors of A.

Therefore, we can compute the first column of U as follows:

u1=1σ1Av1=15[403000][10]=15[430]=[45350]

Since the second singular value is σ2=0, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of U. But we know that U must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors

u=[x1x2x3]

such that u1⋅u=0 and ‖u‖=1.

Solving u1⋅u=0, which is equivalent to 45x1+35x2=0⟹4x1+3x2=0, we get the general solution

[−34x2x2x3]=x2[−3410]⏟b1+x3[001]⏟b2,

where x2 and x3 are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions b1 and b2 are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of U:

u2=[−35450]u3=[001]

So, the matrix U could be the following: U=[45−35035450001]

last_observation.name: Question 12
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the First Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix: Advanced Cases
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{4}{5}{x}_{1}+\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{4} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ \frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{4}{5}{x}_{1}+\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{4} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ \frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

question.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,\sqrt{3}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -\sqrt{3}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{3} \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that if A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of a 3×2 matrix A, then

  • Σ is a 3×2 matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • U is an orthogonal 3×3 matrix,

  • V is an orthogonal 2×2 matrix.

From the matrix Σ, we deduce that σ1=22 and σ2=0. Also, the columns v1 and v2 of V give us the right singular vectors of A.

last_observation.name: Question 13
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the First Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix: Cases Requiring Orthogonalization
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,\sqrt{3}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -\sqrt{3}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{3} \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,\sqrt{3}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -\sqrt{3}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{3} \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

question.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall that if A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of a 3×2 matrix A, then

  • Σ is a 3×2 matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • U is an orthogonal 3×3 matrix,

  • V is an orthogonal 2×2 matrix.

From the matrix Σ, we deduce that σ1=6 and σ2=0. Also, the columns v1 and v2 of V give us the right singular vectors of A.

Therefore, we can compute the first column of U as follows:

u1=1σ1Av1=16[11−1−1−1−1][1212]=16[22−22−22]=[13−13−13]

Since the second singular value is σ2=0, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of U. But we know that U must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors

u=[x1x2x3]

such that u1⋅u=0 and ‖u‖=1.

Solving u1⋅u=0, which is equivalent to 13x1−13x2−13x3=0⟹x1−x2−x3=0, we get the general solution

[x2+x3x2x3]=x2[110]⏟b1+x3[101]⏟b2,

where x2 and x3 are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions b1 and b2 are not mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let c1=b1=[110].

Then, c2=b2−b2⋅c1c1⋅c1c1=[101]−12[110]=12[1−12].

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors c1 and c2, we obtain the second and third columns of U:

u2=[12120],u3=[16−1626]

So, the matrix U could be the following: U=[131216−1312−16−13026]

last_observation.name: Question 14
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the First Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix: Cases Requiring Orthogonalization
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]
$$

  • Σ is a 3×2 matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • U is an orthogonal 3×3 matrix,

  • V is an orthogonal 2×2 matrix.

From the matrix Σ, we deduce that σ1=6 and σ2=0. Also, the columns v1 and v2 of V give us the right singular vectors of A.

Therefore, we can compute the first column of U as follows:

u=[x1x2x3]

feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the following geometric sequence:

$$
-48,\,36,\,-27,\,…
$$

The recursive formula for this geometric sequence is

${a}_{n+1}=${{field-1}}$,\,{a}_{1}=$
{{field-2}}$,\,n\ge 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=-48,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{36}{-48}=-\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-\frac{3}{4}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=-48,\,n\ge 1.
$$

questions.problem:
What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence?

$$
3,\,-12,\,48,\,…
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=3,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{-12}{3}=-4.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-4{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=3,\,n\ge 1.
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence?

$$
24,\,-12,\,6,\,…
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=24,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{-12}{24}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-\frac{1}{2}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=24,\,n\ge 1.
$$

Example: 
                    Constructing a Recursive Formula for a Geometric Sequence
canonical_examples.problem:
What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence?

$$
1, \: 4, \: 16, \: \ldots
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
a_{n+1} = r \cdot a_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}1},$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac 4 1 = {\color{red}4}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
a_{n+1} = {\color{red}4} \cdot a_{n} , \qquad a_1 = {\color{blue}1}, \qquad n\geq 1.
$$

Example: 
                    Calculating a Term of a Geometric Sequence Given Its Recursive Formula
canonical_examples.problem:
What is the $4$th term of the geometric sequence given below?

$$
a_{n+1} = -3 a_n,\qquad a_1 = 2,\qquad n \geq 1
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the recursive formula to compute the terms of the sequence up to the $4$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =2 \\ {a}_{2} & =-3{a}_{1}=-3(2)=-6 \\ {a}_{3} & =-3{a}_{2}=-3(-6)=18 \\ {a}_{4} & =-3{a}_{3}=-3(18)=-54\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a_4 = -54.$

canonical_examples.problem:
What is the $5$th term of the geometric sequence given below?

$$
f(n+1) = -5f(n),\quad f(1) = -1,\quad  n\geq 1
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the recursive formula to compute the terms of the sequence up to the $4$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =-1 \\ f(2) & =-5f(1)=-5(-1)=5 \\ f(3) & =-5f(2)=-5(5)=-25 \\ f(4) & =-5f(3)=-5(-25)=125 \\ f(5) & =-5f(4)=-5(125)=-625\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(5)=-625.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying Geometric Sequences
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $10, \: 20, \: 30, \: 40, \: \dots$

II. $a_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{6}a_n,\quad a_1 = 36,\quad n\geq 1$

III. $f(n+1) = 2f(n)-1,\quad f(1) =2,\quad  n\geq 1$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{20}{10} & =2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{30}{20} & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is a geometric sequence. The recursive rule $a_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{6}a_n$ tells us that each term is $\dfrac{1}{6}$ times the previous term, so the common ratio is $r=\dfrac{1}{6}.$

- Sequence III is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first $3$ terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =2 \\ f(2) & =2\cdot f(1)-1=2\cdot 2-1=3 \\ f(3) & =2\cdot f(2)-1=2\cdot 3-1=5\end{aligned}
$$

The first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(2)}{f(1)}=\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{f(3)}{f(2)}=\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequence II is a geometric sequence.

observed_steps.name: Example: Constructing a Recursive Formula for a Geometric Sequence
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
a_{n+1} = r \cdot a_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}1},$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac 4 1 = {\color{red}4}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
a_{n+1} = {\color{red}4} \cdot a_{n} , \qquad a_1 = {\color{blue}1}, \qquad n\geq 1.
$$

Question 2
?

What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence? 3,−12,48,…

a
an+1=12an,a1=−4,n≥1
b
an+1=−14an,a1=3,n≥1
c
an+1=an−4,a1=7,n≥1
d
an+1=−4an,a1=3,n≥1
e
an+1=−2an,a1=6,n≥1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio r takes the form an+1=r⋅an.

In this case, the first term is a1=3, and we can calculate the common ratio r as

r=a2a1=−123=−4.

Therefore, the recursive formula is

an+1=−4an,a1=3,n≥1.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=64,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{32}{64}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=64,\,n\ge 1.
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence? 5,1,15,…

a
an+1=15an,a1=5,n≥1
b
an+1=an+5,a1=5,n≥1
c
an+1=12an,a1=2,n≥1
d
an+1=5an,a1=5,n≥1
e
an+1=an+15,a1=1,n≥1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio r takes the form an+1=r⋅an.

In this case, the first term is a1=5, and we can calculate the common ratio r as

r=a2a1=15.

Therefore, the recursive formula is

an+1=15an,a1=5,n≥1.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Recursive Formula for a Geometric Sequence
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=24,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{-12}{24}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-\frac{1}{2}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=24,\,n\ge 1.
$$

question.problem:
What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence?

$$
24,\,-12,\,6,\,…
$$
question.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=24,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{-12}{24}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-\frac{1}{2}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=24,\,n\ge 1.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence? 24,−12,6,…

a
an+1=an−36,a1=24,n≥1
b
an+1=−2an,a2=24,n≥1
c
an+1=12an,a1=24,n≥1
d
an+1=−2an,a1=24,n≥1
e
an+1=−12an,a1=24,n≥1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio r takes the form an+1=r⋅an.

In this case, the first term is a1=24, and we can calculate the common ratio r as

r=a2a1=−1224=−12.

Therefore, the recursive formula is

an+1=−12an,a1=24,n≥1.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the following geometric sequence:

$$
-48,\,36,\,-27,\,…
$$

The recursive formula for this geometric sequence is

${a}_{n+1}=${{field-1}}$,\,{a}_{1}=$
{{field-2}}$,\,n\ge 1.$
question.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=-48,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{36}{-48}=-\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-\frac{3}{4}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=-48,\,n\ge 1.
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence?

$$
3,\,-12,\,48,\,…
$$
question.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=3,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{-12}{3}=-4.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-4{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=3,\,n\ge 1.
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence? 3,−12,48,…

a
an+1=12an,a1=−4,n≥1
b
an+1=−14an,a1=3,n≥1
c
an+1=an−4,a1=7,n≥1
d
an+1=−4an,a1=3,n≥1
e
an+1=−2an,a1=6,n≥1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio r takes the form an+1=r⋅an.

In this case, the first term is a1=3, and we can calculate the common ratio r as

r=a2a1=−123=−4.

Therefore, the recursive formula is

an+1=−4an,a1=3,n≥1.

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Recursive Formula for a Geometric Sequence
last_observation.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=3,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{-12}{3}=-4.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-4{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=3,\,n\ge 1.
$$

Question 2
?

What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence? 3,−12,48,…

a
an+1=12an,a1=−4,n≥1
b
an+1=−14an,a1=3,n≥1
c
an+1=an−4,a1=7,n≥1
d
an+1=−4an,a1=3,n≥1
e
an+1=−2an,a1=6,n≥1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio r takes the form an+1=r⋅an.

In this case, the first term is a1=3, and we can calculate the common ratio r as

r=a2a1=−123=−4.

Therefore, the recursive formula is

an+1=−4an,a1=3,n≥1.

feedback.problem:
What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence?

$$
3,\,-12,\,48,\,…
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=3,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{-12}{3}=-4.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-4{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=3,\,n\ge 1.
$$

$$
64,\,32,\,16,\,…
$$

The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=64,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{32}{64}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

$$
{a}_{n+1}=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=64,\,n\ge 1.
$$

a
an+1=15an,a1=5,n≥1
b
an+1=an+5,a1=5,n≥1
c
an+1=12an,a1=2,n≥1

an+1=5an,a1=5,n≥1

an+1=an+15,a1=1,n≥1
Submit

The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio r takes the form an+1=r⋅an.

In this case, the first term is a1=5, and we can calculate the common ratio r as

r=a2a1=15.

Therefore, the recursive formula is

an+1=15an,a1=5,n≥1.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Recursive Formula for a Geometric Sequence
last_observation.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=5,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=\frac{1}{5}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=5,\,n\ge 1.
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:

$$
5,\,1,\,\frac{1}{5},\,…
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence? 5,1,15,…

a
an+1=15an,a1=5,n≥1
b
an+1=an+5,a1=5,n≥1
c
an+1=12an,a1=2,n≥1
d
an+1=5an,a1=5,n≥1
e
an+1=an+15,a1=1,n≥1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio r takes the form an+1=r⋅an.

In this case, the first term is a1=5, and we can calculate the common ratio r as

r=a2a1=15.

Therefore, the recursive formula is

an+1=15an,a1=5,n≥1.
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Recursive Formula for a Geometric Sequence

solution.reasoning: The common ratio is 1/5, since 1÷5=1/5 and (1/5)÷1=1/5. With first term 5, the recursive formula matches option a. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence?

$$
5,\,1,\,\frac{1}{5},\,…
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=5,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=\frac{1}{5}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=5,\,n\ge 1.
$$

feedback.html:
Question 4
?

What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence? 5,1,15,…

a
an+1=15an,a1=5,n≥1
b
an+1=an+5,a1=5,n≥1
c
an+1=12an,a1=2,n≥1
d
an+1=5an,a1=5,n≥1
e
an+1=an+15,a1=1,n≥1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio r takes the form an+1=r⋅an.

In this case, the first term is a1=5, and we can calculate the common ratio r as

r=a2a1=15.

Therefore, the recursive formula is

an+1=15an,a1=5,n≥1.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Recursive Formula for a Geometric Sequence

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence?

$$
24,\,-12,\,6,\,…
$$
question.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=24,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{-12}{24}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-\frac{1}{2}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=24,\,n\ge 1.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence? 24,−12,6,…

a
an+1=an−36,a1=24,n≥1
b
an+1=−2an,a2=24,n≥1
c
an+1=12an,a1=24,n≥1
d
an+1=−2an,a1=24,n≥1
e
an+1=−12an,a1=24,n≥1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio r takes the form an+1=r⋅an.

In this case, the first term is a1=24, and we can calculate the common ratio r as

r=a2a1=−1224=−12.

Therefore, the recursive formula is

an+1=−12an,a1=24,n≥1.

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Recursive Formula for a Geometric Sequence
last_observation.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=24,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{-12}{24}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-\frac{1}{2}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=24,\,n\ge 1.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence? 24,−12,6,…

a
an+1=an−36,a1=24,n≥1
b
an+1=−2an,a2=24,n≥1
c
an+1=12an,a1=24,n≥1
d
an+1=−2an,a1=24,n≥1
e
an+1=−12an,a1=24,n≥1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio r takes the form an+1=r⋅an.

In this case, the first term is a1=24, and we can calculate the common ratio r as

r=a2a1=−1224=−12.

Therefore, the recursive formula is

an+1=−12an,a1=24,n≥1.
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Recursive Formula for a Geometric Sequence

solution.reasoning: The common ratio is (-12)/24=6/(-12)=-1/2, and the first term is 24. Thus option e gives the correct recurrence. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence?

$$
24,\,-12,\,6,\,…
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=24,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{-12}{24}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-\frac{1}{2}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=24,\,n\ge 1.
$$

Solve for $x$ in the figure above given that $\overset{⟷}{AB}∥\overset{⟷}{CD}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the angles $∠JID$ and $∠EJB$ are corresponding angles, they are congruent and therefore have the same measure:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠JID & =m∠EJB \\ 4x+{25}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘}-x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have an equation that we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+{25}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘}-x \\ 5x+{25}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 5x & ={155}^{∘} \\ \frac{5x}{5} & =\frac{{155}^{∘}}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{5}x}{\cancel{5}} & ={31}^{∘} \\ x & ={31}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Solve for $x$ in the figure above given that $\overset{⟷}{AB}∥\overset{⟷}{CD}.$
question.worked_solution:
Since the angles $∠JID$ and $∠EJB$ are corresponding angles, they are congruent and therefore have the same measure:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠JID & =m∠EJB \\ 4x+{25}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘}-x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have an equation that we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+{25}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘}-x \\ 5x+{25}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 5x & ={155}^{∘} \\ \frac{5x}{5} & =\frac{{155}^{∘}}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{5}x}{\cancel{5}} & ={31}^{∘} \\ x & ={31}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠JID & =m∠EJB \\ 4x+{25}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘}-x\end{aligned}

$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$ A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{2t}t \\  & =t{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
$$ A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-5\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((5\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(5\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(5\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+5\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
$$ A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ {{field-1}} ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$
${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ {{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-3t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-3t)={e}^{-3t} \\ r(3t)={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-3t} \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-6t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-4}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

questions.raw_html:
4.Proving Properties of a Fundamental Matrix?

Consider the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant 2×2 matrix. Let Φ(t) be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution x(t) can be written in the form x(t)=Φ(t)c for some constant vector c=[c1,c2]T is given below.

L4: Φ(t)c=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t)

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A\,Φ(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $[a,\,b]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $a$ and $b.$*

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L4}$ and substitution from lines {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ and substitution from line {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\text{L3}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular, 

$$
{x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that ${x}_{2}\text{ is a solution of the system}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L5}.$ By definition, the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column,

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}^{′}(t) & {x}_{2}^{′}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Using ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$ from $\text{L3},$ we substitute each derivative into the matrix to get

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ A{x}_{1}(t) & A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substitution from $\text{L2}\text{ and }\text{L3}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ From $\text{L6}$ we have

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)].
$$

Using the definition $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$ from $\text{L1},$ we substitute to obtain

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by substitution from $\text{L1}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Proving Properties of a Fundamental Matrix
questions.raw_html:
5.Proving Properties of a Fundamental Matrix?

Consider the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant 2×2 matrix. Let Φ(t) be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that Φ(t) satisfies the matrix differential equation Φ′(t)=AΦ(t) is given below.

Hint: [a,b] denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors a and b.

L1: Let Φ(t)=[x1(t),x2(t)]

L2: x1′(t)=Ax1(t)

L3: x2′(t)=Ax2(t)

L4: Φ′(t)=[x1′(t),x2′(t)]

L5: Φ′(t)=[Ax1(t),Ax2(t)]

L6: Φ′(t)=A[x1(t),x2(t)]

L7: Φ′(t)=AΦ(t)

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L3 follows from the fact that
x2 is a solution of the system
x2 is a solution of the system
Φ(t) is invertible for all t
A is diagonalizable
x2 is differentiable

L2 and L3

L1 and L2
L1 and L3
L3 and L4
.

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{2t}t \\  & =t{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-5\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((5\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(5\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(5\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+5\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-3t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-3t)={e}^{-3t} \\ r(3t)={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-3t} \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-6t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$

question.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-3t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-3t)={e}^{-3t} \\ r(3t)={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-3t} \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-6t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\text{L3}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular, 

$$
{x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that ${x}_{2}\text{ is a solution of the system}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L5}.$ By definition, the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column,

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}^{′}(t) & {x}_{2}^{′}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Using ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$ from $\text{L3},$ we substitute each derivative into the matrix to get

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ A{x}_{1}(t) & A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substitution from $\text{L2}\text{ and }\text{L3}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ From $\text{L6}$ we have

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)].
$$

Using the definition $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$ from $\text{L1},$ we substitute to obtain

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by substitution from $\text{L1}.$
