question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{7}xy, & 0\le y\le 1,\,y\le x\le 2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{7}y(4-{y}^{2}), & 0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional variance $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}]$ given that the corresponding expected value is ${\mu }_{X|\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{7}{5}.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{8}{7}xy}{\frac{4}{7}y(4-{y}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2x}{4-{y}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le y\le 1,\,y\le x\le 2.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$

Now, substituting $y=\frac{1}{2}$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,\frac{1}{2})=\frac{2x}{(4-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2})}=\frac{2x}{(\frac{15}{4})}=\frac{8}{15}x.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{8}{15}x\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{15}{\int }_{1/2}^{2}{x}^{3}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{15}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{15}\cdot \frac{1}{4}[{x}^{4}]_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(16-\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{255}{16} \\  & =\frac{17}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}]-{\mu }_{X|\frac{1}{2}}^{2} \\  & =\frac{17}{8}-{(\frac{7}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{17}{8}-\frac{49}{25} \\  & =\frac{33}{200}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting y=12 into the expression for fX|Y(x|y), we get

fX|Y(x|12)=2x(4−(12)2)=2x(154)=815x.

Therefore, we obtain

E[X2|Y=12]=∫−∞∞x2fX|Y(x|12)dx=∫1/22x2⋅815xdx=815∫1/22x3dx=815[x44]1/22=815⋅14[x4]1/22=215(16−116)=215⋅25516=178

Finally,

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{8}{7}xy}{\frac{4}{7}y(4-{y}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2x}{4-{y}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le y\le 1,\,y\le x\le 2.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$

Now, substituting $y=\frac{1}{2}$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,\frac{1}{2})=\frac{2x}{(4-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2})}=\frac{2x}{(\frac{15}{4})}=\frac{8}{15}x.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{8}{15}x\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{15}{\int }_{1/2}^{2}{x}^{3}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{15}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{15}\cdot \frac{1}{4}[{x}^{4}]_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(16-\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{255}{16} \\  & =\frac{17}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}]-{\mu }_{X|\frac{1}{2}}^{2} \\  & =\frac{17}{8}-{(\frac{7}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{17}{8}-\frac{49}{25} \\  & =\frac{33}{200}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{7}xy, & 0\le y\le 1,\,y\le x\le 2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{7}y(4-{y}^{2}), & 0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional variance $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}]$ given that the corresponding expected value is ${\mu }_{X|\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{7}{5}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{8}{7}xy}{\frac{4}{7}y(4-{y}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2x}{4-{y}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le y\le 1,\,y\le x\le 2.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$

Now, substituting $y=\frac{1}{2}$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,\frac{1}{2})=\frac{2x}{(4-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2})}=\frac{2x}{(\frac{15}{4})}=\frac{8}{15}x.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{8}{15}x\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{15}{\int }_{1/2}^{2}{x}^{3}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{15}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{15}\cdot \frac{1}{4}[{x}^{4}]_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(16-\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{255}{16} \\  & =\frac{17}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}]-{\mu }_{X|\frac{1}{2}}^{2} \\  & =\frac{17}{8}-{(\frac{7}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{17}{8}-\frac{49}{25} \\  & =\frac{33}{200}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,3)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2{y}^{7/2}}, & \,1\le y \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables. 
Find the conditional variance $\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=3]$ given that the conditional probability density function ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,3)$ is shown above and the corresponding expected value is ${\mu }_{Y|3}=\frac{5}{3}.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=3] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,3)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2{y}^{7/2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{5}{2{y}^{3/2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[-5\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}]}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=3] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=3]-{\mu }_{Y|3}^{2} \\  & =5-{(\frac{5}{3})}^{2} \\  & =5-\frac{25}{9} \\  & =\frac{20}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=3] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,3)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2{y}^{7/2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{5}{2{y}^{3/2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[-5\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}]}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=3] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=3]-{\mu }_{Y|3}^{2} \\  & =5-{(\frac{5}{3})}^{2} \\  & =5-\frac{25}{9} \\  & =\frac{20}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2(x+2y)}{3}, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1+4y}{3}, & 0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional variance $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=1]$ given that the corresponding expected value is ${\mu }_{X|1}=\frac{8}{15}.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2(x+2y)}{3})}{(\frac{1+4y}{3})} \\  & =\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$ 

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{2(x+2\cdot 1)}{1+4\cdot 1}=\frac{2x+4}{5}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{2x+4}{5})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}+\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{4}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\frac{11}{6}] \\  & =\frac{11}{30}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=1] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=1]-{\mu }_{X|1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{30}-{(\frac{8}{15})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{37}{450}.\end{aligned}

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2(x+2y)}{3})}{(\frac{1+4y}{3})} \\  & =\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$ 

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{2(x+2\cdot 1)}{1+4\cdot 1}=\frac{2x+4}{5}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{2x+4}{5})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}+\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{4}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\frac{11}{6}] \\  & =\frac{11}{30}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=1] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=1]-{\mu }_{X|1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{30}-{(\frac{8}{15})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{37}{450}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2(x+2y)}{3}, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1+4y}{3}, & 0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional variance $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=1]$ given that the corresponding expected value is ${\mu }_{X|1}=\frac{8}{15}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2(x+2y)}{3})}{(\frac{1+4y}{3})} \\  & =\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$ 

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{2(x+2\cdot 1)}{1+4\cdot 1}=\frac{2x+4}{5}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{2x+4}{5})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}+\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{4}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\frac{11}{6}] \\  & =\frac{11}{30}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=1] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=1]-{\mu }_{X|1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{30}-{(\frac{8}{15})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{37}{450}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,4)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{3{y}^{11/3}}, & \,1\le y \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables. 
Find the conditional variance $\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=4]$ given that the conditional probability density function ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,4)$ is shown above and the corresponding expected value is ${\mu }_{Y|4}=\frac{8}{5}.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=4] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,4)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{8}{3{y}^{11/3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{8}{3{y}^{5/3}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{8}{3}{y}^{-5/3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{8}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3}{2})\cdot {y}^{-2/3}]}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & ={[-\frac{4}{{y}^{2/3}}]}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =0-(-4) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=4] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=4]-{\mu }_{Y|4}^{2} \\  & =4-{(\frac{8}{5})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{64}{25} \\  & =\frac{36}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=4] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,4)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{8}{3{y}^{11/3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{8}{3{y}^{5/3}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{8}{3}{y}^{-5/3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{8}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3}{2})\cdot {y}^{-2/3}]}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & ={[-\frac{4}{{y}^{2/3}}]}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =0-(-4) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=4] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=4]-{\mu }_{Y|4}^{2} \\  & =4-{(\frac{8}{5})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{64}{25} \\  & =\frac{36}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/d930c097ed0ddfa454d7f443112c2d9e233e29521e8950fcc4738e742dd3d8dc.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x=\frac{6}{y}$ and $x=7-y$ for $y\in [1,6]$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=-3.$  Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/edea788893771f13f3afc7d9f49e8f1dead4e9b589ca78ef160b9bddccf867c5.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\frac{6}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=7-y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=7-y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/48df22796616a48f9e9ed56474ced12392905e976fdec064b401894f30cbf49b.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}[\,(7-y)-(-3)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[10-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=\frac{6}{y}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/f3240bb3d94231ae5b786b01b2fe11f9e0ea7971978e54f26a4e36b84af71a28.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[\,(\frac{6}{y})-(-3)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[\frac{6}{y}+3]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[10-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[\frac{6}{y}+3]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}({[10-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{6}{y}+3]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/b5ea4fcb15db81b35a8a6e399cc3df734fc1dd41afe42799b8ca2a39734996cb.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x=-\frac{10}{y}$ and $x=y-7$ for $y\in [2,5]$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=-1.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/987999e84c2b22c8b90ecb0381518e7504d0b792ecebb067a7221653422b3e89.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=-\frac{10}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=y-7.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=y-7.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/f8c250c5fbf20980050a1e86f4ac5c91bff7b24bfc7ce5394f33c87703139026.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}[\,(-1)-(y-7)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[6-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=-\frac{10}{y}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/64b440be918c616eb07f05f7f09cb8e14ed649f677afc5f40f66f47ec34ed87e.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[\,(-1)-(-\frac{10}{y})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[\frac{10}{y}-1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[6-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[\frac{10}{y}-1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}({[6-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{10}{y}-1]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/87481d3de1bd3fb02a2fbaa344f120421052335624e8d42b6dd853382b9f764e.png)

The region above enclosed by the curves $y=\sqrt{x}$ and $y={x}^{2}$ for $x\in [0,1]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=-1.$ Find the volume $V$ of the resulting solid. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/bd558d08aa48a17d04b9c3929a5b49a21e5fd7bde8ebfe4a07f8cabfd824b981.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y={x}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/b8c8e0216a8ee045a9d7a570bc26d1765fc54e2110b1c1d2fbbc8f59d1ec22ef.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\sqrt{x})-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[\sqrt{x}+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y={x}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/4cd4e1fb0ad340da9a2e146fa261c6a50e4578f1b77564c8d6a5c6a2f27c81f9.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,({x}^{2})-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[\sqrt{x}+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({(\sqrt{x}+1)}^{2}-{({x}^{2}+1)}^{2})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(2\sqrt{x}-{x}^{4}-2{x}^{2}+x)\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi [(\frac{4}{3}(1)^{3/2}-\frac{1}{5}(1)^{5}-\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3}+\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2})-0] \\  & =\frac{29\pi }{30}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/353b6ad37a77d200719a155e8c14a974f01de00a2e4b4ca3312ce50401a715b7.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x={y}^{2}+2$ and $y=x-4$ for $y\in [-1,2]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-2.$ Find the volume $V$ of the resulting solid. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, since we are rotating about a vertical axis, we need to solve the equation of our second curve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-4\,⟹\,x=y+4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/7e08a30f9ef1f8ce748ba0fcac73f1e93d994e4fd3a3d3d1367568c89c29f4d0.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x={y}^{2}+2,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=y+4.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=y+4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/262546bf3f1d1c9025d23b9fb134c9de7b5299c7b6383563531dffa62244163d.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[\,(y+4)-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[y+6]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x={y}^{2}+2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/cefab13ca3d09fcf596e7906384c2efd1718c289783792f1b0ff950632c823ad.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[\,({y}^{2}+2)-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[{y}^{2}+4]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of our solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}({[y+6]}^{2}-{[{y}^{2}+4]}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}({y}^{2}+12y+36-({y}^{4}+8{y}^{2}+16))\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}(12y+20-{y}^{4}-7{y}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(6{y}^{2}+20y-\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}-\frac{7{y}^{3}}{3})|}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\pi [\,(6\cdot {2}^{2}+20\cdot 2-\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}-\frac{7\cdot {2}^{3}}{3})\,-\,(6-20+\frac{1}{5}+\frac{7}{3})\,] \\  & =\pi (\frac{584}{15}-(-\frac{172}{15})) \\  & =\frac{252\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/ce9f6280200d6f71fc13b4dba705c26341ddf11d369b547e05c8647c0e1c3e8e.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x={y}^{2}-2$ and $x=y$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=3.$ Find the volume $V$ of the resulting solid. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, to determine the limits of integration, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-2 & =y \\ {y}^{2}-y-2 & =0 \\ (y-2)(y+1) & =0 \\ y & =-1,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=-1$ to $y=2.$

Next, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/74e298b85aa9e300d303fa34c761d5ffad214110e315ccf18c33edd2283210ad.png)

The horizontal arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=y,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x={y}^{2}-2.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x={y}^{2}-2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/945dfc9ade4dc95a336f6c0111ea50496242ca60dfddff61f85961547c0c7d3e.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[\,(3)-({y}^{2}-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[5-{y}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/9e25b8fd45f666927edbfec7d9ccd714d14037784f86fb9a8493bf861d521ff9.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[\,(3)-(y)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[3-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}({[5-{y}^{2}]}^{2}-{[3-y]}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}((25-10{y}^{2}+{y}^{4})-(9-6y+{y}^{2}))\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}({y}^{4}-11{y}^{2}+6y+16)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}-\frac{11{y}^{3}}{3}+3{y}^{2}+16y)|}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\pi [(\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}-\frac{11({2}^{3})}{3}+3({2}^{2})+16(2))-(-\frac{1}{5}+\frac{11}{3}+3-16)] \\  & =\pi [\frac{316}{15}-(-\frac{143}{15})] \\  & =\frac{153\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

The region enclosed by the curves x=6y and x=7−y for y∈[1,6] is rotated 360∘ about the line x=−3. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫06([10−y]2−[6y+3]2)dy
b
π∫16([7−y]2−[6y]2)dy
c
π∫16([6y+3]2)dy
d
π∫−6−1([10−y]2−[6y+3]2)dy
e
π∫16([10−y]2−[6y+3]2)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=6y, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=7−y.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=7−y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫16[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫16[(7−y)−(−3)]2dy=π∫16[10−y]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=6y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫16[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫16[(6y)−(−3)]2dy=π∫16[6y+3]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫16[10−y]2dy−π∫16[6y+3]2dy=π∫16([10−y]2−[6y+3]2)dy.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/987999e84c2b22c8b90ecb0381518e7504d0b792ecebb067a7221653422b3e89.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=-\frac{10}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=y-7.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=y-7.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/f8c250c5fbf20980050a1e86f4ac5c91bff7b24bfc7ce5394f33c87703139026.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}[\,(-1)-(y-7)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[6-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=-\frac{10}{y}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/64b440be918c616eb07f05f7f09cb8e14ed649f677afc5f40f66f47ec34ed87e.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[\,(-1)-(-\frac{10}{y})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[\frac{10}{y}-1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[6-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[\frac{10}{y}-1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}({[6-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{10}{y}-1]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

π∫16([6−y]2−[10y−1]2)dy

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫−12[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫−12[(3)−(y)]2dy=π∫−12[3−y]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫−12([5−y2]2−[3−y]2)dy=π∫−12((25−10y2+y4)−(9−6y+y2))dy=π∫−12(y4−11y2+6y+16)dy=π(y55−11y33+3y2+16y)|−12=π[(255−11(23)3+3(22)+16(2))−(−15+113+3−16)]=π[31615−(−14315)]=153π5.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/d930c097ed0ddfa454d7f443112c2d9e233e29521e8950fcc4738e742dd3d8dc.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x=\frac{6}{y}$ and $x=7-y$ for $y\in [1,6]$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=-3.$  Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
question.worked_solution:
Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/edea788893771f13f3afc7d9f49e8f1dead4e9b589ca78ef160b9bddccf867c5.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\frac{6}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=7-y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=7-y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/48df22796616a48f9e9ed56474ced12392905e976fdec064b401894f30cbf49b.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}[\,(7-y)-(-3)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[10-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=\frac{6}{y}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/f3240bb3d94231ae5b786b01b2fe11f9e0ea7971978e54f26a4e36b84af71a28.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[\,(\frac{6}{y})-(-3)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[\frac{6}{y}+3]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[10-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[\frac{6}{y}+3]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}({[10-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{6}{y}+3]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

The region enclosed by the curves x=6y and x=7−y for y∈[1,6] is rotated 360∘ about the line x=−3. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫06([10−y]2−[6y+3]2)dy
b
π∫16([7−y]2−[6y]2)dy
c
π∫16([6y+3]2)dy
d
π∫−6−1([10−y]2−[6y+3]2)dy
e
π∫16([10−y]2−[6y+3]2)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=6y, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=7−y.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=7−y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫16[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫16[(7−y)−(−3)]2dy=π∫16[10−y]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=6y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫16[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫16[(6y)−(−3)]2dy=π∫16[6y+3]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫16[10−y]2dy−π∫16[6y+3]2dy=π∫16([10−y]2−[6y+3]2)dy.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/edea788893771f13f3afc7d9f49e8f1dead4e9b589ca78ef160b9bddccf867c5.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\frac{6}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=7-y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=7-y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/48df22796616a48f9e9ed56474ced12392905e976fdec064b401894f30cbf49b.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}[\,(7-y)-(-3)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[10-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=\frac{6}{y}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/f3240bb3d94231ae5b786b01b2fe11f9e0ea7971978e54f26a4e36b84af71a28.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[\,(\frac{6}{y})-(-3)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[\frac{6}{y}+3]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[10-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[\frac{6}{y}+3]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}({[10-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{6}{y}+3]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

The region enclosed by the curves x=6y and x=7−y for y∈[1,6] is rotated 360∘ about the line x=−3. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫06([10−y]2−[6y+3]2)dy
b
π∫16([7−y]2−[6y]2)dy
c
π∫16([6y+3]2)dy
d
π∫−6−1([10−y]2−[6y+3]2)dy
e
π∫16([10−y]2−[6y+3]2)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=6y, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=7−y.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=7−y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫16[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫16[(7−y)−(−3)]2dy=π∫16[10−y]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=6y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫16[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫16[(6y)−(−3)]2dy=π∫16[6y+3]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫16[10−y]2dy−π∫16[6y+3]2dy=π∫16([10−y]2−[6y+3]2)dy.

solution.reasoning: On 1≤y≤6, 7-y≥6/y. Rotating horizontal slices about x=-3 gives washers with outer radius (7-y)+3=10-y and inner radius 6/y+3. Therefore V=π∫₁⁶[(10-y)²-(6/y+3)²]dy, which is option e. The mathematics is conclusive, but no Math Academy answer key or grading evidence is provided.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/d930c097ed0ddfa454d7f443112c2d9e233e29521e8950fcc4738e742dd3d8dc.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x=\frac{6}{y}$ and $x=7-y$ for $y\in [1,6]$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=-3.$  Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/edea788893771f13f3afc7d9f49e8f1dead4e9b589ca78ef160b9bddccf867c5.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\frac{6}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=7-y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=7-y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/48df22796616a48f9e9ed56474ced12392905e976fdec064b401894f30cbf49b.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}[\,(7-y)-(-3)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[10-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=\frac{6}{y}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/f3240bb3d94231ae5b786b01b2fe11f9e0ea7971978e54f26a4e36b84af71a28.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[\,(\frac{6}{y})-(-3)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[\frac{6}{y}+3]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[10-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}{[\frac{6}{y}+3]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{6}({[10-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{6}{y}+3]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/b5ea4fcb15db81b35a8a6e399cc3df734fc1dd41afe42799b8ca2a39734996cb.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x=-\frac{10}{y}$ and $x=y-7$ for $y\in [2,5]$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=-1.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
question.worked_solution:
Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/987999e84c2b22c8b90ecb0381518e7504d0b792ecebb067a7221653422b3e89.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=-\frac{10}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=y-7.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=y-7.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/f8c250c5fbf20980050a1e86f4ac5c91bff7b24bfc7ce5394f33c87703139026.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}[\,(-1)-(y-7)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[6-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=-\frac{10}{y}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/64b440be918c616eb07f05f7f09cb8e14ed649f677afc5f40f66f47ec34ed87e.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[\,(-1)-(-\frac{10}{y})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[\frac{10}{y}-1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[6-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[\frac{10}{y}-1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}({[6-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{10}{y}-1]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

The region enclosed by the curves x=−10y and x=y−7 for y∈[2,5] is rotated 360∘ about the line x=−1. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫25([y−7]2−[10y]2)dy
b
π∫25([10y−1]2)dy
c
π∫16([6−y]2−[10y−1]2)dy
d
π∫25([6−y]2−[10y−1]2)dy
e
π∫−25([6−y]2−[10y−1]2)dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=−10y, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=y−7.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=y−7.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫25[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫25[(−1)−(y−7)]2dy=π∫25[6−y]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=−10y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫25[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫25[(−1)−(−10y)]2dy=π∫25[10y−1]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫25[6−y]2dy−π∫25[10y−1]2dy=π∫25([6−y]2−[10y−1]2)dy.

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/987999e84c2b22c8b90ecb0381518e7504d0b792ecebb067a7221653422b3e89.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=-\frac{10}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=y-7.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=y-7.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/f8c250c5fbf20980050a1e86f4ac5c91bff7b24bfc7ce5394f33c87703139026.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}[\,(-1)-(y-7)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[6-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=-\frac{10}{y}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/64b440be918c616eb07f05f7f09cb8e14ed649f677afc5f40f66f47ec34ed87e.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[\,(-1)-(-\frac{10}{y})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[\frac{10}{y}-1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[6-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}{[\frac{10}{y}-1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{5}({[6-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{10}{y}-1]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

The region enclosed by the curves x=−10y and x=y−7 for y∈[2,5] is rotated 360∘ about the line x=−1. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫25([y−7]2−[10y]2)dy
b
π∫25([10y−1]2)dy
c
π∫16([6−y]2−[10y−1]2)dy
d
π∫25([6−y]2−[10y−1]2)dy
e
π∫−25([6−y]2−[10y−1]2)dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=−10y, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=y−7.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=y−7.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫25[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫25[(−1)−(y−7)]2dy=π∫25[6−y]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=−10y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫25[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫25[(−1)−(−10y)]2dy=π∫25[10y−1]2dy.

The region above enclosed by the curves $y=\sqrt{x}$ and $y={x}^{2}$ for $x\in [0,1]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=-1.$ Find the volume $V$ of the resulting solid. Do not round the answer.

$V=$

question.worked_solution:
First, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/bd558d08aa48a17d04b9c3929a5b49a21e5fd7bde8ebfe4a07f8cabfd824b981.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y={x}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/b8c8e0216a8ee045a9d7a570bc26d1765fc54e2110b1c1d2fbbc8f59d1ec22ef.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\sqrt{x})-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[\sqrt{x}+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y={x}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226182/assets/4cd4e1fb0ad340da9a2e146fa261c6a50e4578f1b77564c8d6a5c6a2f27c81f9.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,({x}^{2})-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[\sqrt{x}+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({(\sqrt{x}+1)}^{2}-{({x}^{2}+1)}^{2})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(2\sqrt{x}-{x}^{4}-2{x}^{2}+x)\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi [(\frac{4}{3}(1)^{3/2}-\frac{1}{5}(1)^{5}-\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3}+\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2})-0] \\  & =\frac{29\pi }{30}.\end{aligned}
$$

The region enclosed by the curves x=y2−2 and x=y is rotated 2π radians about the line x=3. Find the volume V of the resulting solid. Do not round the answer.
V=
153π5​
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, to determine the limits of integration, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

y2−2=yy2−y−2=0(y−2)(y+1)=0y=−1,2

Hence, our limits of integration are from y=−1 to y=2.

Next, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=y, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=y2−2.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=y2−2.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫−12[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫−12[(3)−(y2−2)]2dy=π∫−12[5−y2]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫−12[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫−12[(3)−(y)]2dy=π∫−12[3−y]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫−12([5−y2]2−[3−y]2)dy=π∫−12((25−10y2+y4)−(9−6y+y2))dy=π∫−12(y4−11y2+6y+16)dy=π(y55−11y33+3y2+16y)|−12=π[(255−11(23)3+3(22)+16(2))−(−15+113+3−16)]=π[31615−(−14315)]=153π5.
